expectedText:
RENTAL APPLICATION SCREENING FEES AND REUSABLE TENANT SCREENING REPORTS (CIV. CODE §§ 1950.6, 1950.1) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory rules on residential rental application screening fees and reusable tenant screening reports as they may apply to an application by Jordan Lee to rent the unit at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 from Pat Morgan. It states what California law provides under Civil Code §§ 1950.6 and 1950.1, what the California Supreme Court said about a pre-statute nonrefundable application charge, and what related state and federal consumer-reporting and fair-housing provisions require when a consumer credit report, an investigative consumer report, or credit history is used in a rental decision. It does not determine whether any fee charged or any screening decision made concerning 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 complied with these provisions, and it does not tell either Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any specific application or dispute.

STATUTORY AUTHORIZATION FOR AN APPLICATION SCREENING FEE AND THE AMOUNT CAP
Civil Code § 1950.6(a) provides that, notwithstanding the security-deposit statute (§ 1950.5), a landlord or the landlord's agent that receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant may charge that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant, subject to the conditions in subdivision (c). The information may include personal reference checks and consumer credit reports; a landlord may, but is not required to, accept and rely on a credit report presented by the applicant. Subdivision (b) caps the fee at the landlord's actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information about the applicant (such as the cost of a tenant screening service or credit reporting service) plus the reasonable value of the landlord's or agent's time spent obtaining that information, and states that in no case may the fee exceed $30 per applicant. That $30 figure may be adjusted annually by the landlord or agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning January 1, 1998.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Notwithstanding Section 1950.5, when a landlord or their agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant, the landlord or their agent may charge, pursuant to subdivision (c), that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant. The information requested and obtained by the landlord or their agent may include, but is not limited to, personal reference checks and consumer credit reports produced by consumer credit reporting agencies as defined in Section 1785.3. A landlord or their agent may, but is not required to, accept and rely upon a consumer credit report presented by an applicant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, authorization of an application screening fee notwithstanding § 1950.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "The amount of the application screening fee shall not be greater than the actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant, including, but not limited to, the cost of using a tenant screening service or a consumer credit reporting service, and the reasonable value of time spent by the landlord or their agent in obtaining information on the applicant. In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the actual-cost limit, the $30 cap, and the annual CPI adjustment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  Known gap: The statute does not itself publish the CPI-adjusted dollar ceiling for any given year, does not specify which Consumer Price Index series is to be used, and does not state who bears the burden of showing the adjustment was computed correctly; this document reports only the $30 base figure and the adjustment mechanism as written and does not state a current dollar maximum. The text quoted is the version amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 29 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026, as it appeared on the Legislature's site on the checked date; earlier versions of subdivisions (a) and (c) differed and were not fetched. The cross-referenced definition of consumer credit reporting agency in § 1785.3 was not fetched.

NO FEE WITHOUT AN AVAILABLE UNIT, AND THE TWO PERMITTED SCREENING-PROCESS STRUCTURES
Civil Code § 1950.6(c)(1) prohibits a landlord or agent from charging an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time. Subdivision (c)(2) further provides that a fee may be charged only if, at the time it is collected, the landlord or agent offers one of two screening processes. The first (subparagraph (A)) requires that completed applications be considered in the order received under the landlord's established screening criteria, that those criteria be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form, that the first applicant meeting the criteria be approved, and that applicants not be charged a fee unless or until their application is actually considered; a fee inadvertently collected because of concurrent submissions does not violate that rule if refunded within seven days to any applicant whose application is not considered (or, at the applicant's option, applied to an application for another of the landlord's units), and no refund is required to an applicant whose application is considered and denied for not meeting the criteria. The second (subparagraph (B)) is a process in which the landlord returns the entire fee to any applicant not selected for tenancy, regardless of reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "A landlord or their agent shall not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, no screening fee when no unit is or will reasonably be available (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "(i) Completed applications are considered, as provided for in the landlord’s established screening criteria, in the order in which the completed applications were received. The landlord’s screening criteria shall be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form. (ii) The first applicant who meets the landlord’s established screening criteria is approved for tenancy. (iii) Applicants are not charged an application screening fee unless or until their application is actually considered."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(c)(2)(A)(i)-(iii) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the first-qualified-in-order process with written screening criteria (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "An application screening process in which the landlord or their agent returns the entire screening fee to any applicant who is not selected for tenancy, regardless of the reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant for tenancy or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(c)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the full-refund-to-non-selected-applicants process (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (c)(2) was part of the text as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026; this document did not fetch the bill or the prior version of the statute and therefore does not describe which portions of subdivision (c) were new in that amendment versus carried over from an earlier amendment. The statute does not define "reasonable period of time" in paragraph (c)(1), does not specify what 'established screening criteria' must contain, and does not state a remedy or penalty for charging a fee without offering one of the two processes; this clause reports the conditions as written and does not address enforcement. Clause (A)(iv) is summarized rather than quoted in full.

ITEMIZED RECEIPT, RETURN OF UNUSED FEE, AND COPY OF THE CREDIT REPORT
Civil Code § 1950.6 imposes three follow-on duties once a screening fee is paid. Under subdivision (d), the landlord or agent must provide the applicant, personally or by mail, a receipt for the fee that itemizes the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent to obtain and process the information about the applicant; the landlord and applicant may agree that the receipt be sent to an email account the applicant provides. Under subdivision (e), if the landlord or agent does not perform a personal reference check or does not obtain a consumer credit report, any amount of the fee not used for the purposes the section authorizes must be returned to the applicant. Under subdivision (f), if a screening fee has been paid, the landlord or agent must provide a copy of the consumer credit report to the applicant who is its subject, by personal delivery, mail, or email, within seven days of receiving the report.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The landlord or their agent shall provide, personally, or by mail, the applicant with a receipt for the fee paid by the applicant, which receipt shall itemize the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord or their agent to obtain and process the information about the applicant. The landlord or their agent and the applicant may agree to have the landlord provide a copy of the receipt for the fee paid by the applicant to an email account provided by the applicant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(d) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the itemized receipt requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "If the landlord or their agent does not perform a personal reference check or does not obtain a consumer credit report, the landlord or their agent shall return any amount of the screening fee that is not used for the purposes authorized by this section to the applicant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(e) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, return of the unused portion of the fee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "If an application screening fee has been paid by the applicant, the landlord or their agent shall provide a copy of the consumer credit report to the applicant who is the subject of that report by personal delivery, mail, or email within seven days of the landlord or their agent receiving the report."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(f) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, copy of the consumer credit report to the applicant within seven days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  Known gap: The statute does not state a deadline for delivering the receipt under subdivision (d) or for returning an unused amount under subdivision (e), and does not specify a remedy for noncompliance with any of these three subdivisions; this clause reports the duties as written. Subdivision (f) refers to 'the consumer credit report' and does not expressly address reports that are not consumer credit reports (for example, an eviction-history or investigative report); the separate copy and notice duties for investigative consumer reports are addressed in a later clause of this document.

WHO IS AN 'APPLICANT,' WHAT AN 'APPLICATION SCREENING FEE' IS, AND WHAT THE FEE IS NOT
Civil Code § 1950.6 supplies its own definitions. 'Landlord' means an owner of residential rental property (subd. (h)). 'Application screening fee' means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application to rent or lease residential rental property (subd. (i)). 'Applicant' means any entity or individual who makes a request to a landlord or agent to rent a residential housing unit, and also any entity or individual who agrees to act as a guarantor or cosignor on a rental agreement (subd. (j)), so a proposed guarantor is a separate 'applicant' for purposes of the per-applicant cap. Subdivision (k) provides that the fee is not an 'advance fee' within the meaning of Business and Professions Code § 10026 and is not 'security' within the meaning of § 1950.5, and subdivision (l) states that the section is not intended to preempt provisions or regulations governing the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "As used in this section, “application screening fee” means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or their agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for the rent or lease of residential rental property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(i) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, definition of 'application screening fee' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "As used in this section, “applicant” means any entity or individual who makes a request to a landlord or their agent to rent a residential housing unit, or an entity or individual who agrees to act as a guarantor or cosignor on a rental agreement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(j) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, definition of 'applicant' including guarantors and cosignors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  "The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5. (l) This section is not intended to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6(k)-(l) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the fee is neither an 'advance fee' nor 'security'; no preemption of housing-assistance program rules (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.6.)
  Known gap: The observation that a guarantor or cosignor is a separate 'applicant' for purposes of the per-applicant cap is this document's reading of the definition in subdivision (j) together with the 'per applicant' language of subdivision (b); no court decision applying the statute that way was located. Business and Professions Code § 10026 (definition of 'advance fee' in the Real Estate Law) was not fetched. Subdivision (g), which states that nothing in the section prevents a landlord from accepting a reusable screening report under § 1950.1, is addressed in the next clause.

REUSABLE TENANT SCREENING REPORTS (CIV. CODE § 1950.1)
Civil Code § 1950.1, added by Stats. 2022, Ch. 288 (AB 2559) and effective January 1, 2023, defines a 'reusable tenant screening report' as a consumer report that was prepared within the previous 30 days by a consumer reporting agency at the applicant's request and expense, is made directly available to a landlord (or provided through a third-party website that regularly provides such reports and complies with state and federal consumer-report law), and is available to the landlord at no cost to access or use. The report must include the applicant's name, contact information, verification of employment, last known address, and the results of an eviction history check conducted in a manner and for a period consistent with applicable law, and it must prominently state the date through which its information is current. A landlord may elect to accept such reports and may require the applicant to state that there has been no material change to the information. If an applicant provides a reusable report to a landlord that accepts them, the landlord may not charge the applicant either a fee to access the report or an application screening fee. The section does not require any landlord to accept reusable reports, does not affect other law on the consideration of criminal history in housing, and yields to any local policy that provides greater protection to applicants.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "(c) A landlord may elect to accept reusable tenant screening reports and may require an applicant to state that there has not been a material change to the information in the reusable tenant screening report. (d) Notwithstanding Section 1950.6, if an applicant provides a reusable tenant screening report to a landlord that accepts reusable tenant screening reports, the landlord shall not charge the applicant either of the following: (1) A fee for the landlord to access the report. (2) An application screening fee."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.1(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, landlord may elect to accept reusable reports; no access fee or screening fee if one is accepted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.1.)
  "(A) Was prepared within the previous 30 days by a consumer reporting agency at the request and expense of an applicant. (B) Is made directly available to a landlord for use in the rental application process or is provided through a third-party website that regularly engages in the business of providing a reusable tenant screening report and complies with all state and federal laws pertaining to use and disclosure of information contained in a consumer report by a consumer reporting agency. (C) Is available to the landlord at no cost to access or use."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.1(e)(6)(A)-(C) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, definition of 'reusable tenant screening report' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.1.)
  "(g) If an ordinance, resolution, regulation, administrative action, initiative, or other policy adopted by a city, county, or city and county conflicts with this section, the policy that provides greater protections to applicants shall apply. (h) This section does not require a landlord to accept reusable tenant screening reports."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.1(g)-(h) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, more-protective local policies control; landlords not required to accept reusable reports (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.1.)
  Known gap: Section 1950.1 does not state what happens if a landlord accepts reusable reports from some applicants but not others, or how a landlord's election to accept such reports is to be communicated; the statute is silent on both points. The cross-referenced criminal-history regulations (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 2, § 12264 et seq.) and the federal definition of 'consumer report' in 15 U.S.C. § 1681a were not fetched for this clause, although § 1681a is fetched and quoted for a different subdivision in a later clause. The five required contents in subdivision (a) and the definition in subdivision (e)(6) are summarized; only subdivisions (c), (d), and (h) are quoted.

BEFORE § 1950.6: NONREFUNDABLE APPLICATION CHARGES AND THE SECURITY-DEPOSIT STATUTE (KRAUS V. TRINITY MANAGEMENT SERVICES)
Section 1950.6 was enacted in 1996 (Stats. 1996, ch. 525, § 1) against the background of the security-deposit statute, Civil Code § 1950.5, which bars nonrefundable deposits. In Kraus v. Trinity Management Services, Inc. (2000) 23 Cal.4th 116, tenants of a San Francisco apartment operator challenged, among other practices, a nonrefundable 'TIER' fee, which the Supreme Court described as a charge for pre-lease administrative services; the trial court had found that the practice violated § 1950.5 and the Unfair Competition Law and had enjoined the defendants from assessing TIER fees or any other nonrefundable charges as a condition of tenancy. The Supreme Court's decision turned on the scope of monetary relief available in a representative Unfair Competition Law action, not on the legality of the fee. In the course of that discussion the court observed that § 1950.6, enacted after the events in suit, now expressly permits a rental application screening fee notwithstanding § 1950.5, and it stated that it therefore did not need to reach the defendants' arguments that § 1950.5 was unconstitutionally vague or that relitigation of the TIER fee's status was barred by res judicata or collateral estoppel.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The first cause of action asserted a violation of Civil Code section 1950.5, which bans nonrefundable security deposits, and was addressed to defendants’ TIER fees, a charge for pre-lease administrative services."
  — Kraus v. Trinity Management Services, Inc. (2000) 23 Cal.4th 116, 23 Cal.4th 116, 122 (statement of the case: the TIER fee and the § 1950.5 cause of action) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1159700/kraus-v-trinity-management-services-inc/)
  "Civil Code section 1950.6, enacted in 1996 (Stats. 1996, ch. 525, § 1) now expressly permits a rental application screening fee “[Notwithstanding Section 1950.5.” Having reached this conclusion, we need not address defendants’ argument that Civil Code section 1950.5 is unconstitutionally vague, either on its face or in its application to"
  — Kraus v. Trinity Management Services, Inc. (2000) 23 Cal.4th 116, 23 Cal.4th 116, 141-142 (court's observation on the later-enacted § 1950.6) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1159700/kraus-v-trinity-management-services-inc/)
  Known gap: Kraus is cited for historical context only: the court did not construe § 1950.6, did not decide whether the TIER fee would have been lawful under it, and its holding concerns Unfair Competition Law remedies (disgorgement into a fluid recovery fund) that are outside this document's subject. The CourtListener text of the opinion renders the court's parenthetical quotation of the statute as “[Notwithstanding Section 1950.5.” with an unmatched opening bracket; the quote is reproduced as it appears in the fetched text, and the bracket is treated as a benign transcription artifact. The opinion text could be fetched only from CourtListener (two fetches with distinct browser header sets, plus phrase-level confirmation via CourtListener's public search); the official reporter was not independently consulted.

ADVERSE-ACTION NOTICE WHEN A CONSUMER CREDIT REPORT IS USED (CIV. CODE § 1785.20; 15 U.S.C. § 1681M)
When a rental decision adverse to the applicant is based in whole or in part on information in a consumer credit report, two adverse-action statutes apply in addition to § 1950.6's copy-of-report duty. California's Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act, Civil Code § 1785.20(a), requires any person taking such adverse action to give the consumer written notice of the action; the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer credit reporting agency that furnished the report; a statement that the decision was based in whole or in part on information in the report; and written notice of the consumer's rights to obtain a free copy of the report within 60 days from that agency and from any nationwide agency, and to dispute the accuracy or completeness of information in it under § 1785.16. A person who shows by a preponderance of the evidence that it maintained reasonable procedures to assure compliance is not liable for a violation (subd. (c)). The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a), imposes parallel duties on any person taking adverse action based on a consumer report, and the federal definition of 'adverse action' in 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(k)(1)(B)(iv) reaches an action or determination made in connection with an application made by, or a transaction initiated by, any consumer, that is adverse to the consumer's interests.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "If any person takes any adverse action with respect to any consumer, and the adverse action is based, in whole or in part, on any information contained in a consumer credit report, that person shall do all of the following: (1) Provide written notice of the adverse action to the consumer. (2) Provide the consumer with the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer credit reporting agency which furnished the report to the person. (3) Provide a statement that the credit grantor’s decision to take adverse action was based in whole or in part upon information contained in a consumer credit report."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1785.20(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, adverse-action notice duties of a user of a consumer credit report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1785.20.)
  "If any person takes any adverse action with respect to any consumer that is based in whole or in part on any information contained in a consumer report, the person shall- (1) provide oral, written, or electronic notice of the adverse action to the consumer;"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a) (Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. Code, current edition), Fair Credit Reporting Act, duties of users taking adverse actions on the basis of information in consumer reports (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section1681m&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "(iv) an action taken or determination that is- (I) made in connection with an application that was made by, or a transaction that was initiated by, any consumer, or in connection with a review of an account under section 1681b(a)(3)(F)(ii) of this title ; and (II) adverse to the interests of the consumer."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(k)(1)(B)(iv) (Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. Code, current edition), Fair Credit Reporting Act, definition of 'adverse action' reaching consumer-initiated applications and transactions (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section1681a&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: Section 1785.20(a) refers to 'the credit grantor's decision' in paragraph (3) although the chapeau applies to 'any person' taking adverse action; this document reads the subdivision as applying to a residential landlord using a consumer credit report, consistent with the chapeau, but located no California appellate decision applying § 1785.20 to a rental application. The FCRA text is quoted from the House Office of the Law Revision Counsel's current edition; the second source (Cornell LII) renders the same words but with an em dash where the OLRC text uses a hyphen and with spaces padding hyperlinked defined terms (for example, 'consumer ,'), so the two copies match only after those typographic variants are normalized. The FCRA's separate credit-score disclosure element in § 1681m(a)(2) and the private-remedy and preemption provisions (15 U.S.C. §§ 1681n, 1681o, 1681t) are not addressed. Civil Code § 1785.16 (dispute rights) and § 1785.3 (definitions) were not fetched.

INVESTIGATIVE CONSUMER REPORTS SOUGHT IN CONNECTION WITH THE HIRING OF A DWELLING (CIV. CODE § 1786.16)
California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act separately regulates 'investigative consumer reports,' which concern a consumer's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living. Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(3) provides that when such a report is sought in connection with the hiring of a dwelling unit (as defined in § 1940(c)), the person procuring it must, not later than three days after the date the report was first requested, notify the consumer in writing that an investigative consumer report will be made regarding those matters; the notice must include the name and address of the agency that will prepare the report and a summary of the consumer's rights under § 1786.22. Under subdivision (b)(1), the person requesting the report must also give the consumer a written means, by a box to check, to indicate that the consumer wishes to receive a copy of any report prepared; if the consumer so indicates, the recipient of the report must send a copy within three business days of the date the report is provided to it, and the copy must contain the name, address, and telephone number of the person who issued the report and how to contact them. Subdivision (b)(2) requires compliance with § 1786.40 if adverse action is a consideration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "If an investigative consumer report is sought in connection with the hiring of a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940, the person procuring or causing the request to be made shall, not later than three days after the date on which the report was first requested, notify the consumer in writing that an investigative consumer report will be made regarding the consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living. The notification shall also include the name and address of the investigative consumer reporting agency that will prepare the report and a summary of the provisions of Section 1786.22."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1786.16(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, written notice within three days when an investigative consumer report is sought for the hiring of a dwelling unit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.16.)
  "(1) Provide the consumer a means by which the consumer may indicate on a written form, by means of a box to check, that the consumer wishes to receive a copy of any report that is prepared. If the consumer wishes to receive a copy of the report, the recipient of the report shall send a copy of the report to the consumer within three business days of the date that the report is provided to the recipient, who may contract with any other entity to send a copy to the consumer. The notice to request the report may be contained on either the disclosure form, as required by subdivision (a), or a separate consent form. The copy of the report shall contain the name, address, and telephone number of the person who issued the report and how to contact them. (2) Comply with Section 1786.40, if the taking of adverse action is a consideration."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1786.16(b)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, check-box request for a copy of the report; three-business-day delivery; adverse-action cross-reference (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.16.)
  Known gap: Which tenant-screening products constitute 'investigative consumer reports' (as opposed to consumer credit reports governed by § 1785.20) depends on the definitions in § 1786.2, which was not fetched; this clause reports the dwelling-unit notice and copy duties as written without characterizing any particular screening product. Section 1786.22 (consumer's rights to inspect files), § 1786.40 (adverse-action duties for investigative reports), § 1786.12(d) (permissible purposes), and § 1940(c) (definition of 'dwelling unit') are cross-referenced but were not fetched.

CREDIT HISTORY AND INCOME STANDARDS WHERE A GOVERNMENT RENT SUBSIDY IS INVOLVED (GOV. CODE § 12955(O))
The Fair Employment and Housing Act, as amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 776 (SB 267) effective January 1, 2024, adds a screening-specific rule to the list of unlawful housing practices in Government Code § 12955. Under subdivision (o)(1), where there is a government rent subsidy it is unlawful to use a financial or income standard for rental eligibility that is not based on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant, or to use a person's credit history as part of the application process without offering the applicant the option, at the applicant's discretion, of providing lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of a reasonable ability to pay the tenant's portion of the rent, such as government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements. If the applicant elects to provide such evidence, the housing provider must give the applicant reasonable time to respond with it and must reasonably consider it in lieu of credit history in deciding whether to offer the rental. Subdivision (o)(2) preserves the owner's ability to request information or documentation to verify employment, to request landlord references, and to verify identity, and § 12955(p)(2) states that a written or oral inquiry concerning the level or source of income is not itself source-of-income discrimination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "(1) In instances in which there is a government rent subsidy, to do either of the following: (A) Use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for the rental of housing that is not based on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant. It states what California law provides under Civil Code §§ 1950.6 and 1950.1, what the California Supreme Court said about a pre-statute nonrefundable application charge, and what related state and federal consumer-reporting and fair-housing provisions require when a consumer credit report, an investigative consumer report, or credit history is used in a rental decision. Civil Code § 1950.6(a) provides that, notwithstanding the security-deposit statute (§ 1950.5), a landlord or the landlord's agent that receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant may charge that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant, subject to the conditions in subdivision (c). The information may include personal reference checks and consumer credit reports; a landlord may, but is not required to, accept and rely on a credit report presented by the applicant. Subdivision (b) caps the fee at the landlord's actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information about the applicant (such as the cost of a tenant screening service or credit reporting service) plus the reasonable value of the landlord's or agent's time spent obtaining that information, and states that in no case may the fee exceed $30 per applicant. That $30 figure may be adjusted annually by the landlord or agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning January 1, 1998.
